paper_a.title: A Simple Unpredictable Pseudo-Random Number Generator

paper_b.title: Theory and Applications of Trapdoor Functions

metadata.description: Blum-Blum-Shub (BBS) and Yao independently establish cryptographically secure pseudorandom generators based on number-theoretic hardness assumptions. BBS gives a concrete construction (the x^2 mod N generator) and proves its unpredictability under the Quadratic Residuacity Assumption; Yao develops a general theory of effective entropy, perfectness (computational indistinguishability from uniform), and shows that any stable one-way function yields a perfect PRG, including a quadratic-residue PRG instance. The papers are parallel rediscoveries of the PRG-from-hardness paradigm, with Yao providing the abstract framework and BBS the concrete number-theoretic instantiation.

matches.explanation: Both define a pseudorandom (sequence) generator as a polynomial-time procedure that takes a short seed and outputs a long sequence. BBS's 'pseudo-random sequence generator' on a seed space and Yao's 'pseudorandom number generator' both require poly-time computation and short input/long output; the difference is bookkeeping (BBS via seed-space ensemble, Yao via integer parameters $k,n$).

BBS's $x^2 \bmod N$ generator (squaring on quadratic residues mod $N=PQ$ with $P,Q\equiv 3\bmod 4$, output parity bit per iterate) is exactly the same construction Yao references in his quadratic-residue PRG (AP300.1) and his factoring trapdoor (ExP300.7). Yao's pseudocode iterates $x_{i+1}=f(N,x_i)$ and outputs parity bits, then XORs $(\log n)^2$ such streams; the inner generator is identical to BBS.

BBS's abstract triple $(X,T,B)$ formalism (a measure-preserving transformation $T$ on the seed space plus a partition $B$ that reads one output symbol) has no direct counterpart in Yao. Yao formalizes generators via probabilistic algorithms and one-way functions rather than via measure-preserving dynamical-systems machinery.

The $1/P$ generator (base-$b$ quotient digits of $r/P$) is a paper-specific construction in BBS that Yao never discusses. BBS uses it as a foil (predictable, hence not cryptographically secure) leading up to the $x^2 \bmod N$ generator.
Generalized de Bruijn sequences are BBS-specific structural concepts used to characterize the $1/P$ generator output; Yao does not consider de Bruijn-style structure.

BBS defines $\epsilon$-advantage for a parity-guesser / left-predictor; Yao defines polynomial statistical tests and what it means for a source to pass them. Both formalize 'an efficient adversary's deviation from uniform random'. BBS is targeted (next-bit / previous-bit prediction with explicit advantage $\epsilon$); Yao is the more general 'pass every poly-time test' formulation (which by his Theorem 3 = perfectness).

Special primes / Sophie-Germain-style prime chains and 'special $N$' are BBS-specific number-theoretic conditions used to control the period $\lambda(\lambda(N))$ of the orbit. Yao does not analyze period structure.

Both papers state the discrete logarithm intractability assumption and define the discrete log problem. Yao gives two formulations (Assumption BM via Blum-Micali, AssumP300.2; and his own circuit-size version, AssumP300.5 / DP300.33). BBS's AssumP299.1 is a uniform-procedure version; the underlying mathematical assumption is the same.

Both papers state the Quadratic Residuacity Assumption (QRA) and define the QR problem. BBS's AssumP299.2 is a probabilistic-procedure formulation; Yao's Assumption GM (AssumP300.1) is a circuit-size formulation. Both are attributed to Goldwasser-Micali and assert hardness of deciding quadratic residuacity mod $N$ on a non-negligible fraction of inputs.

Yao's intractability-of-factoring assumptions (AssumP300.3, AssumP300.4) have no direct analog in BBS. BBS works under QRA and only mentions factoring through the connection to backwards-jump (TP299.11). Yao uses factoring hardness directly to instantiate trapdoor functions.
Theorem that the $1/P$ generator yields generalized de Bruijn sequences is a structural result on BBS's foil generator, with no counterpart in Yao.
Theorem 2 (poly-time predictability of $1/P$ generator) is BBS-specific: it shows the $1/P$ generator is broken, motivating the move to $x^2 \bmod N$. Yao does not analyze the $1/P$ construction.

BBS's lemma on the unique-quadratic-residue square root for $P,Q \equiv 3 \bmod 4$ is a number-theoretic ingredient specific to the BBS construction; Yao does not state this lemma explicitly (he uses the same fact implicitly via Rabin's trapdoor and his factoring trapdoor).

BBS's reduction lemma (parity-guessing advantage converts to QR-guessing advantage) is the key hard-core-bit step in BBS's proof. Yao does not prove this specific reduction; his Theorem 8 (perfect PRG from stable one-way functions) is the higher-level abstract analog but does not explicitly carry out a parity-bit hardcore argument for QR.
BBS's backwards-jump algorithm (compute $x_{-1}$ given factorization, via Tonelli + CRT) is an internal algorithmic contribution of BBS; Yao does not give a backwards-jump algorithm.

BBS's TP299.4 ($x^2 \bmod N$ generator is poly-time unpredictable to the left under QRA) and Yao's TP300.10 (any stable one-way function yields a perfect PRG) play the same role: each is the paper's main 'cryptographic security' theorem for a PRG. BBS's is concrete (specific generator, specific assumption, predict-previous-bit security); Yao's is abstract (any stable one-way function, perfectness in his sense). The instantiation of Yao's TP300.10 to factoring/QR yields essentially BBS's result.

BBS's TP299.5 (the $x^2 \bmod N$ sequences pass every poly-time statistical test, modulo QRA, in the sense of Yao) is explicitly cited as 'in the sense of Yao' and aligns with Yao's TP300.5 (statistical-test characterization of perfectness) plus TP300.6 (information-theoretic characterization). BBS uses Yao's framework as the very definition of indistinguishability/perfectness; this is the strongest cross-paper signal of parallel rediscovery / framework reuse.

BBS's proof sketch of TP299.5 explicitly says 'following Yao' and uses Yao's predictor-from-distinguisher hybrid argument. The proof is BBS's, but its technique is borrowed from Yao; we record it here as 'none' on the matches side since Yao's proof appears as PP300.1 against TP300.12, not against TP300.5.

BBS's results on the period of the $x^2 \bmod N$ orbit ($\pi \mid \lambda(\lambda(N))$, conditions for equality, special-$N$ sufficient conditions) are a substantial number-theoretic contribution unique to BBS; Yao does not analyze orbit periods.
Period-finding algorithm given $\lambda(\lambda(N))$ and its factorization is BBS-specific.
Random-access (jump forward / backward to the $i$-th iterate given $\lambda(N)$) theorems are BBS-specific algorithmic contributions; Yao does not consider random access into the PRG sequence.
BBS's reduction 'oracle for $(\pi, x_{-i})$ enables factoring' is a paper-specific result connecting the BBS generator to factoring; Yao does not state an analog.

Pair-guessing security (no efficient procedure can guess any (location, bit) pair of generator output given $x_{k+1}$) is a strengthened security result in BBS Section 10; Yao does not state this strengthening.

BBS's Alice-Bob public-key protocol example (using $x^2 \bmod N$ generator + backwards-jump for decryption) is conceptually the same as Yao's probabilistic public-key cryptosystem (PPKC) construction from a trapdoor function (TP300.11). Both achieve a public-key encryption scheme by combining a trapdoor (factoring of $N$) with a PRG, then XORing the PRG output with the message. BBS gives an explicit instance; Yao gives the general theorem.
Yao's formal definition of 'computationally secure cryptosystem' via $H_C(M) \approx H_C(M|J)$ has no explicit BBS counterpart; BBS works at the level of unpredictability of generator bits.

Yao's source / source ensemble / channel-coding-scheme / expected-channel-cost definitions are part of his information-theoretic framework (Part 1) and have no BBS analog. BBS's DP299.1/DP299.2 (seed domain, seed space) are loosely related as 'parameterised probability families', but the framing differs enough that we mark them as separate paper-original contributions on each side rather than aligning them.

BBS's seed domain + accessible distribution (DP299.1+DP299.2) and Yao's 'uniform source ensemble' (DP300.11) both formalize 'a parameterised family of admissible inputs of given length plus a distribution'. The match is loose: BBS's distribution is required to be efficiently sampleable but not necessarily uniform on equal-length strings, while Yao's uniform ensembles are specifically uniform-on-fixed-length-strings. Marked low-confidence and analogous.
Yao's $(t,k)$-encoding, $(t,k)$-entropy sequence, effective entropy $H_e(S)$, and true-random ensemble $T_0$ are the core information-theoretic contributions of his Part 1, with no analogue in BBS.
Effective entropy lower bound (Yao Theorem 1) is internal to Yao's framework.
Effective entropy of the true-random ensemble $T_0$ is internal to Yao's framework.
Yao's effective Shannon Second Theorem (Theorem 2) is part of his information-theoretic framework with no BBS analog.
Lower bound on channel cost is internal to Yao's framework.

Yao's witness algorithm and indistinguishable source ensemble definitions are the foundational notion of computational indistinguishability. BBS reuses the underlying intuition (statistical-test-passing) but does not redefine these primitives; they are paper-original contributions of Yao.
Yao's notion of perfect uniform source ensemble is a paper-specific foundational definition. BBS uses 'passes every poly-time statistical test' (citing Yao) rather than redefining perfectness.

'Perfect pseudorandom number generator' is Yao's defined term; BBS uses 'unpredictable' / 'passes every test'. The two map onto each other (via Yao's TP300.5/6) but the formal definitions are separate.
Effective conditional entropy / mutual information / effective independence are Yao's information-theoretic framework, absent in BBS.
Symmetric effective independence (Yao Theorem 5) is internal to Yao's information-theoretic framework.
Yao's Theorem 6 (independence via indistinguishability) is internal to Yao's framework.
Polynomial-time distribution ensemble, correlation ensemble, induced distribution are Yao's framework objects with no direct BBS analog.

Yao's general definition of one-way function and stable one-way function (Definitions 22 and 24) is the abstract central object of Yao's paper. BBS does not define one-way functions abstractly, working only with the concrete squaring map.

Yao's one-way function with a key, abstract trapdoor function (DP300.30), and strong one-way function (DP300.32) are abstractions of the cryptographic primitives. BBS uses concrete instantiations (factoring + squaring) without naming them as instances of these abstract types.

Trapdoor function (informal, attributed to Diffie-Hellman) is cited external in Yao but discussed extensively as a Yao contribution in formalising it. BBS does not introduce trapdoor-function terminology.
Yao's inversion characterization of one-wayness (Theorem 7) is internal to his framework.
Yao's Corollary 'computationally secure cryptosystem from stable one-way functions' has no BBS analog at this level of abstraction (BBS gives a concrete protocol example ExP299.5 instead).

Yao's derandomization theorems (strong one-way functions / factoring hardness / discrete-log hardness imply $R \subseteq \bigcap DTIME(2^{n^\epsilon})$) are unique to Yao; BBS does not address derandomization.
